messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Niko was 21, a European American man working as a public defender, and he had been in a relationship for just over a year when he came for help. He described himself as someone who had learned early to keep moving, to stay useful, and to avoid being a burden, but after fleeing as a refugee and arriving in the United States, he found that ordinary life did not feel ordinary to him anymore. The event he kept returning to happened during the escape: the crowded, disorganized stretch of travel in which he was surrounded by unfamiliar people, noise, and uncertainty, unable to know what would happen next. He did not talk about the full details with others, and even in session he kept circling the edges of it, as if naming too much would make it more real. What stayed with him most clearly were pictures rather than a full story — fragments of faces, a cramped space, and the look and feel of being trapped in a moment that could not be escaped. When the memory surfaced, he often felt his body slip back into the same position it had been in then, tightening in the same way, as though his muscles remembered before he could fully describe it. At other times, the event came back not as an image but as a wave of the same terror, abrupt and complete, with no clear scene attached to it.

In the months after arriving, Niko began watching his own thoughts closely, worried that if he let his mind drift in the wrong direction he might go “crazy” or lose control. He described checking himself constantly, almost second by second, for signs that something was wrong with him. He also made a point of not talking about what had happened or what came after it. Friends and his partner noticed that he would shut down when the conversation moved anywhere near the journey, immigration, or people being trapped or detained. He was also careful to avoid reminders that came from other people, including comments, news stories, or casual questions that touched on refugees or border crossings. He said it felt safer to steer away quickly than to risk being pulled back into the event.

At work, these patterns became harder to hide. As a public defender, Niko spent his days in offices, hallways, and courtrooms where unexpected noises were common. A phone dropping in a neighboring cubicle, a file cabinet slamming, or a door snapping shut made him jump harder than the people around him. He knew the reaction was out of proportion, which embarrassed him, but he could not stop it. In the quiet moments between meetings, when the office went unusually still, he found himself on edge, waiting for something to happen. Silence did not soothe him; it made him feel that danger was about to break in. In court, he sometimes reacted as though he were in immediate trouble even when nothing was wrong, feeling his body tighten before he had time to register that he was safe.

Niko had also come to believe that the world itself was dangerous. He said he had to be on guard all the time and especially careful because you never know what can happen next. That belief showed up in the way he moved through the day: scanning rooms, noticing exits, and feeling that he could not fully relax even when he was with people he trusted. His partner had tried to be supportive, but Niko’s reluctance to talk meant that she often only saw the edge of what he was carrying. He would go quiet if she asked questions about the past, and he preferred not to have reminders of it in the home. Over time, this made him feel more separate and more tired, as if he were always preparing for the next unknown thing while trying not to let anyone see how much energy that took.

By the time he sought treatment, the symptoms had become impossible to ignore. His PCL-5 score reflected how much distress he was experiencing, but what brought him in was more immediate: he was exhausted by the constant sense that something bad might happen, unsettled by how easily ordinary sounds threw him, and frightened by the moments when the memory arrived as raw emotion or body sensation without warning. He said he wanted help because he was tired of monitoring himself so closely and tired of living as if the danger had never ended. What he hoped for was not to forget what happened, but to be able to sit through a quiet room, hear a sudden noise, and stay present with his partner and at work without feeling as if he were back in the moment of escape.
